[OBJECTIVE]: The purpose of this study is to determine whether tracheostomy stomal maturation affects the risk of tracheocutaneous fistula (TCF) in children.
[METHODS]: A retrospective chart review was conducted for all children who both underwent a tracheostomy and were decannulated between 2012 and 2021 at a tertiary children's hospital. Charts were analyzed for demographics, surgical technique, and development of a TCF. TCF was defined as a persistent fistula following 3 months after decannulation.
[RESULTS]: 179 children met inclusion criteria. Stomal maturation was not significantly associated with the risk of TCF, including on multivariable analysis adjusting for age at tracheostomy and duration of tracheostomy (p = 0.089).

Title: Duration of tracheostomy dependence and development of tracheocutaneous fistula in children.

Journal/Date: The Laryngoscope (2017)

MeSH Keywords: Child, Child, Preschool, Cutaneous Fistula, Device Removal, Female, Humans, Infant, Infant, Newborn


--- ABSTRACT ---
[OBJECTIVE]: To determine whether the risk of developing a tracheocutaneous fistula (TCF) increases with longer tracheostomy dependence times in children.
[STUDY DESIGN]: Retrospective review of medical records.
[METHOD]: A retrospective chart review was conducted for all children who both underwent tracheotomy and were decannulated between 2002 and 2011 at a tertiary children's hospital. Charts were analyzed for duration of tracheostomy and evidence of TCF up to 12 months. Data for these criteria was available on 164 out of 182 patients.
[RESULTS]: A significant difference in the duration of tracheostomy dependence between children with and without resultant TCF was determined by the Wilcoxon signed rank test (P = 0.0003). The relative risk (RR) of a persistent TCF was significantly increased when the duration of tracheostomy dependence was greater than 24 months (RR = 2.5217, P < 0.005) when compared to those decannulated before 12 months. The mean tracheostomy dependence times for children with and without TCF were 33.1 and 23.4 months, respectively. Overall, 94 children (57.3%) developed a TCF.
[CONCLUSION]: To our knowledge, this study represents the largest collection of data for children who have been decannulated following tracheostomy placement. These data demonstrate that the risk of developing a TCF increases with longer tracheostomy dependence times in children.
[LEVEL OF EVIDENCE]: 4. Laryngoscope, 127:2709-2712, 2017.

Maturation of the stoma was performed in 88 (59.1%) of the 149 tracheostomies. There was an overall complication rate of 21.5% (32/149, not including granulation tissue formation). There were 9 (6.0%) early complications and 23 (15.4%) late complications. The overall incidence of tracheocutaneous fistulas occurred in 11 (11.2%) of the 98 decannulated patients: 6 (10.2%) of the 59 matured stomas and 5 (12.8%) of the 39 nonmatured stomas. Granulation tissue was found on subsequent laryngoscopy in 24 (27.3%) of the 88 matured stomas versus 23 (37.7%) of the 61 nonmatured stomas. There were no tracheostomy-related mortalities. Maturing the tracheostomy stoma resulted in a decreased morbidity from accidental decannulations and did not increase the incidence of tracheocutaneous fistulas or granulation tissue formation.

key_findings.finding: In the strongest direct pediatric study (179 children, retrospective, 2012–2021), stomal maturation was not significantly associated with persistent TCF after adjustment for age at tracheostomy and duration of tracheostomy (multivariable p=0.089). Overall, 98/179 (54.7%) developed TCF and 107/179 (60.0%) had matured stomas; the authors concluded maturation did not affect TCF risk.

source_tools.relevance: Direct adjusted comparison of stomal maturation and TCF

key_findings.finding: An earlier pediatric retrospective series (264 tracheostomies; 133 planned decannulations) likewise found no significant increase with maturation: persistent TCF occurred in 47/89 (53%; reported cohort rate 27%) after maturation versus 20/44 (45%; reported cohort rate 22%) without maturation; P=0.44 for TCF and P=0.80 for decannulation. This is compatible with no causal increase, but the nonrandomized groups may differ in baseline risk.

source_tools.relevance: Direct matured versus nonmatured pediatric comparison

key_findings.finding: A pediatric surgical series of 149 tracheostomies found TCF in 6/59 (10.2%) decannulated patients with matured stomas versus 5/39 (12.8%) with nonmatured stomas, concluding maturation did not increase TCF; maturation was also associated with fewer accidental decannulations. This study did not establish that groups were comparable for duration or other confounders.

Duration of cannulation is a much more consistent predictor than maturation. In 164 children, TCF risk was significantly higher when tracheostomy dependence exceeded 24 months versus less than 12 months (RR 2.5217, P<0.005); mean duration was 33.1 months with TCF versus 23.4 months without. A separate 129-child multivariable study found persistent TCF associated with longer tracheostomy duration, younger age at placement, and tracheobronchomalacia.

The biologic rationale is that persistent TCF reflects epithelialization of a chronically maintained tract, but the available clinical studies do not show that surgically maturing the skin-to-trachea stoma itself causes more epithelialization or fistula persistence. Maturation is plausibly confounded by age, indication, anatomy, expected duration of dependence, and institutional surgical practice; the 2024 study's adjustment for age and duration attenuated concern for an independent maturation effect.

Adult-specific incidence evidence directly comparing stomal maturation versus no maturation was not identified in the retrieved literature. An adult TCF repair series (14 patients; mean tracheostomy duration 8.1±4.7 months) addresses surgical management rather than incidence or maturation causality, and reviews describe prolonged cannulation/multiple tracheostomies as risk factors. Thus, conclusions are substantially stronger for children than adults.
